messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Retired
- Trauma Type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
- Pcl5: 66

She is 68, North American, married for more than four decades, and retired after years of working in public schools. Before her life divided into a before and after, her days move with an easy predictability. She and her husband wake early, drink coffee in the kitchen, argue lightly over the crossword, and make plans they no longer have to squeeze around work schedules. Retirement feels hard-won and ordinary in the best way. Their grown children call often. She keeps a neat house, tends tomato plants in summer, and likes the comfort of knowing where he is in the next room.

The rupture comes on an ordinary Tuesday. Her husband leaves to run a quick errand and does not come home. At first she is irritated by the delay, then puzzled, then seized by a dread she cannot name. The phone rings from an unfamiliar number. A stranger’s voice is too calm. There has been an accident. She remembers the drive to the hospital in fragments: red lights that seem personally cruel, her hands slipping on the steering wheel, the thought repeating with primitive certainty, no, no, no. By the time she arrives, he is already gone.

She still describes that day as if it is happening in flashes rather than as a memory. The emergency department smell of antiseptic and burnt coffee makes her stomach clench even now. She sees the nurse’s mouth moving before she hears words. She notices absurd details she cannot forget—the crease in the sheet, one of his shoes set crooked on the floor, a vending machine humming in the hallway. She does not cry at first. She feels split open and unreal, as though she is watching a woman in sensible shoes receive the worst news of her life.

In the first weeks after his death, people fill the house with casseroles, sympathy cards, and stories about what a good man he is. She thanks everyone. She handles paperwork, chooses flowers, signs forms, and answers questions in a voice she barely recognizes. At night, though, the shock breaks into terror. She jerks awake after brief stretches of sleep, heart pounding, certain the phone is ringing again. Sometimes she dreams she is back in the hospital corridor, trying to run and getting nowhere. Sometimes she dreams he is at the door and feels, for one sweet second after waking, that none of it happened. The second after that is unbearable.

Months pass, and the world seems offended by how normal it expects her to be. Neighbors say she is strong. Her children worry because she stops driving unless absolutely necessary. The route past the intersection where the accident happened becomes impossible; even hearing the street name makes her chest tighten. Sirens send her into a cold sweat. If she sees flashing lights in her rearview mirror, she grips the wheel so hard her hands ache. She begins to avoid the grocery store at busy times because she cannot tolerate the sudden noise of carts crashing or announcements over the loudspeaker. She tells people she is “just tired,” but inside she is braced for catastrophe every minute.

She starts arranging her life around safety. She checks locks repeatedly before bed. She keeps her phone charged and within reach, volume turned high, though the ring itself can make her jump. When her adult son is ten minutes late, she imagines twisted metal and emergency rooms. She calls, then hates herself for calling. News reports of accidents hook her attention against her will. She does not want to look, but she cannot look away. The world now feels random and predatory, as if disaster waits just outside the frame of ordinary life.

The loss is not only fear; it is also the cruel persistence of his absence. She still sets two plates out sometimes, then stands in the kitchen staring at what she has done. His coat remains in the hall closet because touching it feels both necessary and impossible. She talks to his photograph when the house gets too quiet. Yet she also avoids parts of him. She cannot sort through the box of hospital papers. She has not returned to the restaurant where they had their last anniversary dinner. When friends begin telling funny stories about him, she smiles tightly and changes the subject, because once his face rises clearly in her mind, it brings the whole day of his death with it.

Retirement, which once promised spaciousness, now gives too much room for memory. Without the structure of work, mornings stretch long and vulnerable. She used to volunteer at the library, but she stops after realizing she cannot focus on a page for more than a few minutes. Her concentration frays in small humiliating ways—misplacing keys, rereading the same paragraph, forgetting why she has opened a cupboard. She feels older than her age, not in her body so much as in her spirit. She is easily startled, often irritable, then ashamed of it. Her daughter says she seems far away even when she is sitting right there.

In session, she speaks carefully, as if language itself might trigger an avalanche. She says she misses her husband every hour, but what disturbs her most is not only that he died. It is that the moment of learning it shattered her sense that life is basically safe, that ordinary afternoons lead to ordinary evenings. She wants to remember their marriage—its jokes, routines, loyalties—but the memory that comes first is always the phone call, the drive, the hallway, the shoe on the floor. She lives with him and loses him again each day, caught between yearning for the past and scanning for the next disaster.
